records.table: Monkey Shoulder Blended Malt Scotch Whisky is the Speyside blend that William Grant & Sons made to mix: single malts only, no grain, from first-fill bourbon casks. Expect citrus, vanilla and malt, and pour it over ice, long with soda or stirred in a Rob Roy.
records.story: The name comes from the malting floor. Maltmen once turned germinating barley by hand, and the repeated strain could leave a shoulder that hung low, which the trade called a monkey shoulder. William Grant & Sons, the family firm that makes Glenfiddich and The Balvenie, took the name for a blend of single malts with no grain whisky in it. By one account work on the recipe began in 2003; the whisky went on sale in Britain and France in 2005, built from three of the firm's Speyside malts: Glenfiddich, The Balvenie and Kininvie. It was made with bartenders and mixed drinks in mind, and it reached the United States in 2012. In 2017 a peated version, Smokey Monkey, joined it. The firm no longer names the malts in each batch, so tell the three distilleries as the blend's origin, not as its recipe. Behind the bar it is the bottle that puts the words blended malt in front of many guests, and it shows that malt whisky can be a working spirit: over ice, lengthened with soda, stirred into a Rob Roy.

records.table: Compass Box The Peat Monster is a blended malt from a London house that distils nothing and blends the malts it buys, mostly Caol Ila. Pour it neat: coastal smoke, lemon and iodine over pear and vanilla, bottled at 46 per cent.
records.story: Compass Box was founded in London in 2000 by an American who had worked in marketing for Johnnie Walker, and its early blends were made in his west London home. The house has no distillery of its own: it buys whisky from Scottish distillers, chooses its casks and blends. By its own account The Peat Monster grew out of Monster, a blend it made in 2003 for a New York shop, and it is bottled at 46 per cent. In 2005 the house released The Spice Tree, a malt given a second maturation with inner staves of French oak, and the Scotch Whisky Association held the method outside the rules because it was not a traditional one. The house later remade the whisky with French oak cask heads in place of the staves. In 2015 it clashed with the Association again, this time over publishing the full make up of its blends, which the rules on age statements did not allow, and it argued in public for the right to tell a buyer more. When it trimmed its core range in 2024, The Spice Tree went and The Peat Monster stayed. For a bartender it is the lesson in how a blender builds smoke from parcels, and in what an honest recipe on the label can teach.

records.story: Douglas Laing & Co. began in Glasgow in 1948 as a family firm that blended whisky bought from distillers, and in time it came to bottle single casks under its own names as well. In 2009 it released Big Peat, the first of what became its Remarkable Regional Malts, a set of blended malts each drawn from one whisky region of Scotland. Big Peat takes Islay's malts and nothing else: by the producer's account Caol Ila brings sweetness, Bowmore balance, Ardbeg an earthy, medicinal edge and Port Ellen a degree of elegance. Port Ellen had closed in 1983, so whatever share of it went into a bottle had been distilled before then; the distillery was rebuilt and reopened in March 2024. In 2013 the two brothers who had run the firm for some forty years divided it, and Big Peat stayed with Douglas Laing & Co. Older and finished editions have followed under the same name, but the bottle a guest asks for is the plain one at 46 per cent. For a bartender it is the clear lesson in what a region gives: Islay smoke and salt without one distillery's name on the front.

records.story: Naked Grouse was first released in 2011 by the makers of The Famous Grouse, as a blended Scotch finished in first-fill sherry casks. In 2017 its recipe dropped grain whisky and it became a blended malt, drawing on single malts that Edrington then made, among them The Macallan, Highland Park and The Glenrothes. In 2021 Edrington renamed it Naked Malt, to make plain that it is a blended malt, and the trade reported the recipe unchanged. In September 2024 Edrington agreed to sell The Famous Grouse and Naked Malt to William Grant & Sons, and the sale was completed on 1 July 2025, so the label passed to the house that makes Monkey Shoulder. Through the change of name the method held: a marriage of malts given a last six months or more in Oloroso casks that had never held whisky. For a bartender it is the counterweight to a bourbon-cask blended malt such as Monkey Shoulder: the same rule of malts only, read through sherry wood, with dried fruit and toffee where the other shows citrus and vanilla.

records.table: Shackleton Blended Malt Scotch Whisky is a Highland blended malt from Whyte & Mackay, built on the remaking of the whisky taken to Antarctica on the Nimrod expedition of 1907. Expect vanilla, honey and orchard fruit with a whisper of bonfire smoke.
records.story: Ernest Shackleton (1874 to 1922) sailed for Antarctica in 1907 on the Nimrod expedition, and among its stores were cases of Mackinlay's Rare Old Highland Malt, by later accounts distilled at Glen Mhor in Inverness. The party wintered in 1908 in a hut it built at Cape Royds, and when it left, the whisky stayed behind. Conservators of the New Zealand Antarctic Heritage Trust found crates beneath the hut and, in January 2010, lifted five: three marked as Mackinlay's whisky and two as brandy. In 2011 bottles were flown to Scotland, where the master blender of Whyte & Mackay, the firm that by then held the Mackinlay's name, drew a sample through a cork with a syringe, studied it and built a replica from the firm's malts at the original strength of 47.3 per cent. Glen Mhor itself had closed in the 1980s. In 2017 the firm released Shackleton Blended Malt Scotch Whisky, a lasting blended malt of Highland malts at 40 per cent, built on that replica: first in airport shops, then in Britain and France, and late that year in the United States. For a bartender it shows how a blender reads an old whisky and rebuilds it from what lies in the warehouse.
